title: The Mu'allaqa of al-Nabigha
intro: The diwan introduces this ode as an appeal to al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir, king of al-Hira, after words about the queen, al-Mutajarrida, were reported to him. From Mayya's deserted camp the poet sets out on a she-camel whose speed brings to mind a wild bull facing a pack of hounds. He asks the king to judge with the discernment of a woman who once counted a flock of doves in flight. An oath of innocence and the image of the Euphrates in flood bring him back to the pardon he seeks.

translation: Home of Mayya, on the heights above the slope,
you stand deserted. Long ages have passed over you.
1.sharh: He addresses the site where Mayya lived as though she might answer through it. Its position is still clear after all those years, although the people who gave it meaning are gone.

translation: I stopped there towards evening to question it.
It could give no answer. No one was in the camp
2.sharh: For a moment the dwelling seems to struggle for an answer. The empty ground accounts for the silence and leads his eye to the few things he can still recognise.

translation: except horse tethers I could barely make out,
and a bank like a basin cut in hard, unbroken ground.
3.sharh: The ties mark where horses once stood. The low bank that kept runoff out of a tent has survived the tent itself, visible like the rim of a basin laboriously dug in hard soil.

translation: She drew its scattered earth back round it.
The girl's hoe packed the damp soil firm.
4.sharh: The earthwork lets him reconstruct someone's movements. A girl has scraped back its loose outer edges and beaten the wet earth down so it will hold.

translation: She let the oncoming runoff find its course
and banked the earth up to the curtains and stacked gear.
5.sharh: The girl gives the water the bank had held back a way through. In the diwan commentary what she brings up to the tent curtains is the earth that shields the household gear.

translation: By evening it was empty, its people gone.
What laid Lubad low has laid this place waste.
6.sharh: As suddenly as he pictured the camp alive, it is empty again. Lubad was the last of Luqman's proverbially long-lived vultures. Even that life ran out.

translation: Leave what you see. There is no bringing it back.
Hoist the saddle frame onto a tough, wild-ass-like she-camel,
7.sharh: He breaks off his own vigil with two orders, to let the ruins go and to lift the saddle. The she-camel has the hardiness of a wild ass.

translation: thick with firm flesh. Her full-grown tooth
creaks like a wooden pulley running on rope.
8.sharh: The crowded muscle gives a sense of the animal's bulk. The grating of her mature tooth brings in the familiar sound of a well rope rubbing the wood of its pulley.

translation: My saddle, as the day wore past its height,
seemed at al-Jalil to ride a lone, watchful bull,
9.sharh: No change of mount has taken place. The speed of the camel carries his imagination to a solitary wild bull, alert to the slightest sign of danger.

translation: one of Wajra’s wild herd, its shanks picked out in colour,
lean in the belly like a polisher’s matchless blade.
10.sharh: The bull comes into focus by degrees, from the patches of colour on its lower legs to its lean, gleaming outline. A sword fresh from the polisher gives that outline an edge.

translation: A night cloud travelled over it from al-Jawza'.
The north wind drove hard hail against it.
11.sharh: The constellation marks the quarter from which the weather comes. Alone through the night, the bull has already endured the driving hail before the hounds appear.

translation: A huntsman’s voice startled it. All night it had
fear and cold enough to gladden its enemies.
12.sharh: The huntsman's voice gives the bull a second reason to shiver. In Abu Ubayda's reading, its state is everything those who wish it ill could have hoped for.

translation: He loosed them at it. The bull was carried on
by tight-knit joints, free of stiffness.
13.sharh: The hunter releases his pack and the sentence changes subject as the bull runs. Its escape depends on sound legs with tightly made joints.

translation: Dumran was close when his master urged him on,
within striking distance of a fighter at bay.
14.sharh: The hound has been urged within reach of the bull. A fighter hemmed into a last refuge gives the measure of how dangerous that short distance is.

translation: The bull thrust a horn clean through the hound’s flank,
as a horse doctor lances an ailing shoulder.
15.sharh: The horn enters the fleshy part behind the shoulder. What recalls the veterinary surgeon is the exactness of the thrust into the affected place.

translation: Sticking out through the side of the hound, it looked
like a drinkers’ roasting spit forgotten by their fire.
16.sharh: The exposed tip makes the horn look like the end of a roasting spit. The forgotten spit by a party's fire fixes the terrible stillness after the thrust.

translation: Hunched up, the hound gnawed the tip of the horn,
fast on something jet-black, solid and straight.
17.sharh: The impaled hound can still use its jaws. Curling in to bite the horn only brings its teeth against that hard black point.

translation: When Washiq saw his companion killed outright,
with no blood payment due and no life to claim,
18.sharh: The surviving hound watches its companion die. Blood money and retaliation belong to human society, and the poet lends the hound that vocabulary to express the finality of the loss.

translation: his own mind said, “I see nothing to gain.
Your friend has neither come through safe nor caught his prey.”
19.sharh: Washiq takes the other hound's fate as a warning. His imagined inner voice makes an account of the chase from the hunter's side, with nothing won and a life lost.

translation: That she-camel will bring me to al-Nu'man,
whose bounty reaches people near and far.
20.sharh: “That one” picks up the she-camel after the long chase. Only now does he name the man to whom her speed must carry him.

translation: Among men I see no one whose deeds resemble his,
and I make no exception among the peoples
21.sharh: He makes the king's conduct the standard, then seems to rule out every possible equal. The sentence runs straight into one extraordinary exception.

translation: except Solomon, when God said to him,
“Rise among my creatures and restrain them from wrong.
22.sharh: Solomon is the exceptional king in this comparison. The first words put into God's mouth concern a ruler's responsibility for the people in his care.

translation: Subdue the jinn. I have given them leave
to build Tadmur with stone slabs and pillars.
23.sharh: The verse makes the monumental stonework of Tadmur, or Palmyra, visible evidence of Solomon's command over the jinn. It draws on a legend about the city's builders.

translation: Whoever obeys you, reward him for his obedience
as he obeyed, and show him the right path.
24.sharh: The obedient subject is owed a benefit corresponding to his service and guidance for the future. The advice has a bearing on the poet's own claim to loyal treatment.

translation: Whoever defies you, punish him with a punishment
that checks the wrongdoer. Harbour no grudge.”
25.sharh: The stated purpose of punishment is to stop injustice. The command ends by distinguishing that public duty from a private resentment that might outlast it.

translation: Save for your like, or one you draw ahead of
as a thoroughbred wins at the finishing post,
26.sharh: He turns to address al-Nu'man directly. Anyone who might come close in merit still follows him home, as the second horse follows the winner at the post.

translation: no one gives a choice she-camel with such welcome gifts following,
gifts freely given, with nothing grudged.
27.sharh: The comparison of givers begun several verses earlier now reaches the gift itself. A fine she-camel comes with further gifts and no unpleasant obligation attached.

translation: Giver of a hundred stout camels, made handsome
by the sa'dan of Tudih in their thick coats,
28.sharh: Tudih's pasture has put flesh on the camels and dressed them in dense coats. The king gives a hundred head of visibly well-fed stock.

translation: and pale camels, broken in, their elbows well out,
girt with new saddles from al-Hira,
29.sharh: The pale riding camels have been trained. Their elbows stand clear of their sides for an easy stride, and they come equipped with new saddles from the royal city.

translation: and women stepping out with their fine robes trailing,
kept cool at noon, like gazelles on bare ground,
30.sharh: The women listed among the royal gifts have lived sheltered from the midday heat. On bare ground every movement of a gazelle is visible, like theirs beneath their trailing robes.

translation: and horses surging eagerly against their reins
like birds escaping a squall of hail.
31.sharh: The reins make the horses' forward pull perceptible. A flock suddenly racing the hail gives an equivalent for their burst of speed.

translation: Judge as the young woman of the tribe judged
when she saw a flock of doves coming to the shallow pool.
32.sharh: He asks the king to judge his case as accurately as the young woman could judge the size of a moving flock. She has only the time it takes the birds to fly past on their way to water.

translation: The two walls of a ridge enclosed them. She followed them
with an eye like glass, never salved for soreness.
33.sharh: Between the sides of a ridge the flock bunches together. Glass evokes a clear, undimmed eye, able to distinguish birds where ordinary sight might find a blur.

translation: She said, “If only we had these doves,
with our own dove, and half as many more. Enough.”
34.sharh: She words the calculation as a wish. The three quantities are the flying flock, half that flock again and the single dove already hers.

translation: They reckoned it and found it as she had reckoned,
ninety-nine, neither one fewer nor one more.
35.sharh: The ninety-nine include the extra half flock in her wish. Al-Tibrizi works the sum out as sixty-six birds in the air plus another thirty-three.

translation: With her own dove she made a hundred.
How swiftly she had reckoned that number.
36.sharh: Her single dove completes the hundred. The point for the king is how quickly an exact judgment can be made by someone who sees clearly.

translation: No, by the life of him whose Ka'ba I have touched,
and by the blood poured over the altar stones,
37.sharh: He stakes his word on a shrine he has touched and the blood of animals sacrificed at standing stones. These are the religious institutions familiar to the pre-Islamic speaker.

translation: and by him who keeps the sheltering birds safe,
whom Mecca’s riders stroke between al-Ghayl and al-Sa'ad,
38.sharh: The birds have come to the sanctuary for protection. Their tameness under a traveller's hand gives the threatened speaker an image of what it means to have safe conduct.

translation: I said none of the evil reported to you.
If I did, may my hand never lift my whip to me.
39.sharh: His denial ends in a curse on himself should it prove false. Lifting a riding whip is so ordinary a movement that losing it would mean losing the use of his hand.

translation: It was the talk of people whose words brought me grief.
What they said beat against my liver.
40.sharh: The slander has passed from someone else's lips into his own body. The liver, a seat of powerful feeling in Arabic poetry, takes the blows.

translation: Word reached me that Abu Qabus had threatened me.
No one rests with a lion roaring.
41.sharh: Abu Qabus is al-Nu'man. Like a lion's roar, the threat can reach its hearer and drive him from his rest long before its source is in sight.

translation: Be patient. May all the peoples ransom you,
and all the wealth and children I gather.
42.sharh: He asks the king to hold his hand long enough to hear him. The lavish formula of ransom ends in the most personal things the poet could give up.

translation: Do not cast at me a weight no one could meet,
even if my enemies close round you in mutual support.
43.sharh: The king's power would fall on him like a mass of rock. His accusers close round the king as hearthstones surround a pot, each reinforcing the others.

translation: Even the Euphrates, when winds stir it
and its high waves fling foam against both banks,
44.sharh: The comparison is suspended while he builds a picture of the river in flood. Wind roughens the surface until foam reaches both banks.

translation: fed by every brimming, roaring watercourse
with heaps of yanbut shrubs and snapped branches,
45.sharh: Every tributary adds its noise and volume to the Euphrates. The heaped-up shrubs and broken branches show what the flood has torn loose upstream.

translation: while the frightened boatman clings to his pole,
worn out and streaming with sweat,
46.sharh: The view moves into a boat. The pole in the exhausted boatman's hands brings the force of all that water down to what one man can barely hold.

translation: is never more generous than his freely flowing bounty.
What he gives today leaves tomorrow’s giving whole.
47.sharh: Only now does the sentence begun with the Euphrates reach its point. Today's gift takes nothing from the next day's supply.

translation: Here is my praise. If you hear good in it,
I have hinted at no reward, O king.
48.sharh: Praise at court commonly called for a gift in return. He interrupts his denial of such a motive with the ceremonial salutation due to a king.

translation: Here is my plea. If it does me no good,
the man who brings it must keep company with misery.
49.sharh: He places the finished ode before the king as his defence. Its speaker can name the consequence of rejection, but the king's answer lies beyond the poem.

1.1.3.head: مَيَّة
1.1.3.meaning: Mayya, the woman whose former home he addresses.

1.1.4.head: العَلياء
1.1.4.meaning: The high ground on which the camp once stood.

1.1.5.head: السَّنَد
1.1.5.meaning: The rising slope at the side of a valley.

1.2.1.head: أَقوى
1.2.1.meaning: To stand deserted, of a place its people have left.

2.1.3.head: أُصَيلان
2.1.3.meaning: Towards evening. Al-Tibrizi also transmits a wording meaning “at evening, to question it”.

2.2.1.head: عَيَّ
2.2.1.meaning: To be at a loss for an answer, here of a dwelling addressed as a person.

2.2.4.head: الرَّبع
2.2.4.meaning: A former campsite or dwelling place.

3.1.2.head: الأَواريّ
3.1.2.meaning: Horse tethers or tethering stakes left at a campsite.

3.1.3.head: لَأي
3.1.3.meaning: Slowness and difficulty, the effort it takes to discern old traces.

3.2.1.head: النُّؤي
3.2.1.meaning: A low earthen bank round a tent to keep runoff from entering.

3.2.3-4.head: المَظلومَة الجَلَد
3.2.3-4.meaning: “Wronged, hard ground”, ground dug for a basin where digging is unusual and difficult.

4.1.1.head: رَدَّ
4.1.1.meaning: Brought the loose earth back. A passive reading makes the earth itself the subject.

4.2.2.head: الوَليدَة
4.2.2.meaning: The young female servant who maintains the bank around the tent.

4.2.3.head: المِسحاة
4.2.3.meaning: A hoe or spade for digging and scraping earth together.

4.2.5.head: الثَّأَد
4.2.5.meaning: Damp earth that packs down under the hoe.

5.1.3.head: أَتِيّ
5.1.3.meaning: Runoff coming from elsewhere, also explained as a small watercourse.

5.2.3.head: السِّجفان
5.2.3.meaning: The two curtains hanging across the front of a tent.

5.2.4.head: النَّضَد
5.2.4.meaning: Household goods stacked one upon another.

6.1.5.head: اِحتَمَلَ
6.1.5.meaning: To strike camp and leave with one's household and belongings.

6.2.1.meaning: To lay waste or wear away, here of time working on a place.

6.2.6.head: لُبَد
6.2.6.meaning: Lubad, the last of Luqman's legendary vultures, proverbial for a long life that still came to an end.

7.1.1.head: عَدِّ
7.1.1.meaning: Pass on and leave the subject of the ruins behind.

7.2.2.head: القُتود
7.2.2.meaning: The wooden pieces of a camel's saddle frame.

7.2.4.head: عَيرانَة
7.2.4.meaning: A she-camel whose strength recalls a wild ass.

7.2.5.head: أُجُد
7.2.5.meaning: A firmly built she-camel with a powerful back.

8.1.2-3.head: دَخيس النَّحض
8.1.2-3.meaning: “Close-packed flesh”, dense muscle covering the frame.

8.1.4.head: بازِل
8.1.4.meaning: The tooth whose emergence marks maturity in a camel, here heard grating.

8.2.4.head: القَعو
8.2.4.meaning: A wooden pulley or the wood that holds its wheel.

8.2.5.head: المَسَد
8.2.5.meaning: A twisted rope running across a well pulley.

9.2.2.head: الجَليل
9.2.2.meaning: Al-Jalil, the place in this reading. The name can also refer to thumam grass.

9.2.4.head: مُستَأنِس
9.2.4.meaning: An animal keeping a wary lookout, here the wild bull.

10.1.3.head: وَجرَة
10.1.3.meaning: Wajra, a stretch of open country associated in poetry with wild game.

10.1.5.head: أَكارِع
10.1.5.meaning: The lower legs or shanks, here marked with contrasting colours.

10.2.2.head: المَصير
10.2.2.meaning: The gut. Its being drawn in gives the bull a lean belly.

10.2.4.head: الصَّيقَل
10.2.4.meaning: A polisher who brings a sword blade to a bright finish.

11.1.4.head: الجَوزاء
11.1.4.meaning: Al-Jawza', a constellation associated in older Arabic weather lore with the coming of rain.

11.1.5.head: سارِيَة
11.1.5.meaning: A rain cloud travelling by night.

11.2.1.head: أَزجى
11.2.1.meaning: Drove or urged along, of wind driving hail against the bull.

12.1.4.head: كَلّاب
12.1.4.meaning: A huntsman in charge of a pack of hounds.

12.2.1-2.head: طَوع الشَّوامِت
12.2.1-2.meaning: “What ill-wishers desire”. Another explanation takes shawamit as the legs on which he stood all night.

13.2.1-2.head: صُمع الكُعوب
13.2.1-2.meaning: Slender legs with close, firm joints, the bull's means of escape.

13.2.5.head: الحَرَد
13.2.5.meaning: A disorder of the leg sinews that spoils an animal's gait.

14.1.2.head: ضُمران
14.1.2.meaning: Dumran, the hound that comes within reach of the bull's horn.

14.1.5.head: أَوزَعَ
14.1.5.meaning: To set a hound on its quarry.

14.2.4.head: المُحجَر
14.2.4.meaning: A last refuge, a position in which a fighter is hemmed in.

14.2.5.head: النَّجُد
14.2.5.meaning: Brave, a description of the fighter in the diwan commentary.

15.1.2.head: الفَريصَة
15.1.2.meaning: The fleshy part near the shoulder that quivers in fright.

15.1.3.head: المِدرى
15.1.3.meaning: A pointed implement, here the bull's horn.

15.2.2.head: المُبَيطِر
15.2.2.meaning: A veterinary surgeon, pictured opening the affected part with a lancet.

15.2.6.head: العَضَد
15.2.6.meaning: An ailment of an animal's upper foreleg or shoulder.

16.2.1.head: سَفّود
16.2.1.meaning: A roasting spit, the likeness of the horn projecting through the hound.

16.2.2.head: شَرب
16.2.2.meaning: A party of drinkers gathered together.

16.2.5.head: مُفتَأَد
16.2.5.meaning: The place where a fire is made for roasting meat.

17.1.2.head: عَجَمَ
17.1.2.meaning: To bite or gnaw at something hard.

17.2.4.head: صَدق
17.2.4.meaning: Firm, unyielding, of the hard substance of the horn.

18.1.3.head: واشِق
18.1.3.meaning: Washiq, the second hound, who sees Dumran killed.

18.2.4.head: عَقل
18.2.4.meaning: Blood money due to the kin of a slain person.

18.2.6.head: قَوَد
18.2.6.meaning: Retaliation for a killing, a life claimed for a life.

19.2.2.head: مَولى
19.2.2.meaning: A companion or ally, the hound lost in the chase.

19.2.6.head: صادَ
19.2.6.meaning: To catch one's quarry. The shortened verb follows a negative.

20.1.3.head: النُّعمان
20.1.3.meaning: Al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir, king of al-Hira and addressee of the poem.

20.2.7.head: البَعَد
20.2.7.meaning: Those far away, paired with people close to the king.

21.2.2.head: حاشى
21.2.2.meaning: To except anyone from a judgment.

22.1.2.head: سُلَيمان
22.1.2.meaning: Solomon, the prophet and king whose command extends to the jinn.

22.2.4.head: اُحدُد
22.2.4.meaning: Restrain, keep the people in one's charge from going wrong.

22.2.6.head: الفَنَد
22.2.6.meaning: Folly or error in judgment and conduct.

23.1.1.head: خَيِّس
23.1.1.meaning: Subdue, put the jinn under one's command.

23.2.2.head: تَدمُر
23.2.2.meaning: Tadmur, or Palmyra, a city in the Syrian desert whose buildings legend associated with Solomon's jinn.

23.2.3.head: الصُّفّاح
23.2.3.meaning: Broad, flat slabs of building stone. The reciter uses the form with an initial u given by al-Tibrizi. The form with i has the same meaning.

24.1.3.head: اِنفَع
24.1.3.meaning: Benefit or reward him for obeying. Another reading says to honour him.

25.2.2.head: الظَّلوم
25.2.2.meaning: A persistent wrongdoer whom punishment is meant to deter.

25.2.4-6.head: قَعَدَ عَلى ضَمَد
25.2.4-6.meaning: “Sat nursing a grudge”, harboured anger after the occasion for punishment.

26.2.2.head: الجَواد
26.2.2.meaning: A fine, fleet horse in a race.

26.2.6.head: الأَمَد
26.2.6.meaning: The finishing mark that determines which horse has won.

27.1.2.head: فارِهَة
27.1.2.meaning: A choice she-camel, or more generally a fine gift followed by other favours.

27.2.6.head: نَكَد
27.2.6.meaning: Meanness or grudging constraint in the giving of a gift.

28.1.3.head: المِعكاء
28.1.3.meaning: Stout, well-fleshed camels. Another recension gives young she-camels.

28.2.1.head: سَعدان
28.2.1.meaning: Sa'dan, a pasture plant on which camels fatten and which catches in their coats.

28.2.2.head: توضِح
28.2.2.meaning: Tudih, the grazing ground named for its sa'dan.

28.2.5.head: اللِّبَد
28.2.5.meaning: Thick, matted locks of camel hair.

29.1.1.head: الأُدم
29.1.1.meaning: Light-coloured she-camels, a class prized for riding.

29.1.4-5.head: فُتل المَرافِق
29.1.4-5.meaning: “Elbows turned out”, a build that gives the legs room to move freely.

29.2.3.head: الحيرَة
29.2.3.meaning: Al-Hira, the Lakhmid royal city in Iraq from which the saddles come.

30.1.3.head: الرَّيط
30.1.3.meaning: Fine, single-piece garments whose hems trail as the women move.

30.1.4.head: فانَقَ
30.1.4.meaning: Kept them in comfort. The first consonant belongs to the verb. Al-Tibrizi gives another form of the same root with the same sense.

30.2.4.head: الجَرَد
30.2.4.meaning: Bare open country in which a gazelle is fully visible.

31.1.2.head: مَزَعَ
31.1.2.meaning: To spring or run forward at speed.

31.1.3.head: غَرب
31.1.3.meaning: Keen energy or impetus as the horses run.

31.2.4.head: الشُّؤبوب
31.2.4.meaning: A sudden hard squall, here carrying hail.

32.1.3-4.head: فَتاة الحَيّ
32.1.3-4.meaning: “The young woman of the tribe.” Abu Ubayda identifies her as Zarqa' al-Yamama, famous for her eyesight. In the account al-Asma'i heard from Bedouin informants, she is the daughter of al-Khuss.

32.2.3.head: شِراع
32.2.3.meaning: Heading for a watering place, also glossed as gathering together. Al-Nahari reads shira'. Another text has sira', swift.

32.2.5.head: الثَّمَد
32.2.5.meaning: A shallow pool or small reserve of water to which the doves are flying.

33.1.3.head: نيق
33.1.3.meaning: A high ridge whose sides narrow the space around the flock.

33.2.6.head: الرَّمَد
33.2.6.meaning: Inflammation of the eyes, for which a salve would be applied.

34.1.3.meaning: If only. The particle ma allows two traditional case readings for the doves and their half share.

34.2.4.head: قَد
34.2.4.meaning: Enough, that would suffice. The word closes the woman's wish.

35.1.1.head: حَسَّبَ
35.1.1.meaning: To count up carefully and test her reckoning.

35.1.2.head: أَلفى
35.1.2.meaning: To find something to be as it was described.

36.2.2.head: حِسبَة
36.2.2.meaning: A reckoning, here one made in a flash.

37.1.5.head: الكَعبَة
37.1.5.meaning: The Ka'ba, the sanctuary at Mecca invoked in the oath.

37.2.4.head: الأَنصاب
37.2.4.meaning: Standing stones at which sacrifices were made.

37.2.6.head: جَسَد
37.2.6.meaning: Blood, the old sense here of sacrificial blood on the stones.

38.1.1.head: المُؤمِن
38.1.1.meaning: The giver of safety, invoked for protecting the birds in the sanctuary.

38.1.2.head: العائِذات
38.1.2.meaning: Birds that have taken refuge under the protection of the shrine.

38.2.4-5.head: الغَيل وَالسَّعَد
38.2.4-5.meaning: Al-Ghayl and al-Sa'ad, local names near Mecca. Al-Asma'i understood ghayl as running water, Abu Ubayda ghil as a thicket.

39.1.6-7.head: أُتِيَ بِهِ
39.1.6-7.meaning: “It was brought to you”, said to the king who received the damaging report.

39.2.4.head: سَوط
39.2.4.meaning: A rider's whip, an everyday test of the very hand he puts under the curse.

40.2.3.head: قَرع
40.2.3.meaning: A beating, here the bodily impact he gives to a slanderous report.

40.2.5.head: الكَبِد
40.2.5.meaning: The liver, traditionally a seat of deep feeling and grief.

41.1.3-4.head: أَبو قابوس
41.1.3-4.meaning: Abu Qabus, the familiar name of al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir.

41.2.4.head: زَأر
41.2.4.meaning: The roar of a lion, heard here in the king's threat.

42.1.2.head: فِداء
42.1.2.meaning: A ransom or life offered for someone, here in a formal expression of devotion.

42.2.2.head: ثَمَّرَ
42.2.2.meaning: To accumulate or increase, here one's wealth and family.

43.1.3.head: رُكن
43.1.3.meaning: A support or strong point, here an overwhelming force the king could bring to bear.

43.1.5.head: كِفاء
43.1.5.meaning: A match, an equal in strength.

43.2.2.head: تَأَثَّفَ
43.2.2.meaning: To surround as the hearthstones surround a pot, of accusers closing round the king.

43.2.4.head: الرِّفَد
43.2.4.meaning: Mutual assistance lent by the accusers to one another.

44.1.2.head: الفُرات
44.1.2.meaning: The Euphrates, seen here in its seasonal violence in flood.

44.2.2.head: غَوارِب
44.2.2.meaning: Wave crests, named for the high part of a camel's back.

44.2.3.head: العِبران
44.2.3.meaning: The two banks struck by the river's foam.

45.1.4.head: مُترَع
45.1.4.meaning: Full to the brim, of a valley contributing its water.

45.1.5.head: لَجِب
45.1.5.meaning: Loud with the roar of running water.

45.2.4.head: اليَنبوت
45.2.4.meaning: Yanbut, a plant or shrub swept along by the flood.

45.2.5.head: الخَضَد
45.2.5.meaning: Broken or bent branches and other vegetation.

46.2.1.head: الخَيزُرانَة
46.2.1.meaning: A flexible cane, here understood as the boatman's punting pole.

46.2.3.head: الأَين
46.2.3.meaning: Exhaustion after struggling to handle the boat.

46.2.4.head: النَّجَد
46.2.4.meaning: Sweat brought out by distress and exertion.

47.1.4-5.head: سَيب نافِلَة
47.1.4-5.meaning: “An outpouring over and above”, a gift given beyond what is owed.

48.2.3-4.meaning: “May you refuse a curse”, a salutation to a king who scorns deeds that might deserve one.

48.2.5.head: الصَّفَد
48.2.5.meaning: A gift or recompense, particularly the reward a poet might receive for praise.

49.1.3.meaning: This, an old feminine demonstrative pointing to the plea he has just delivered.

49.1.4.head: عِذرَة
49.1.4.meaning: A plea in one's defence intended to lift blame.

49.2.4.head: النَّكَد
49.2.4.meaning: Misfortune or a wretched condition. Another ending leaves him wandering the land.
